definition: The welfare maximization problem is an optimization problem studied in economics and computer science.
details: Its goal is to partition a set of items among agents with different utility functions, such that the welfare – defined as the sum of the agents' utilities – is as high as possible. In other words, the goal is to find an item allocation satisfying the utilitarian rule. An equivalent problem in the context of combinatorial auctions is called the winner determination problem. In this context, each agent submits a list of bids on sets of items, and the goal is to determine what bid or bids should win, such that the sum of the winning bids is maximum.

explainer.lead: Welfare maximization is an optimization problem: partition items among agents with different utility functions so that the sum of utilities is as high as possible. It matters because it formalizes the utilitarian rule for fair and efficient allocation.

tiers.eli5: Imagine splitting a pile of things among friends so that, added up, everyone is as happy as possible with what they got.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to frame allocation and auction design, where each agent submits bids on sets of items and the goal is to pick the winning bids. A pitfall is that the general problem is hard to solve exactly, so practical systems rely on approximations or restricted bid structures.
tiers.paperLevel: Find an allocation of a set of items to agents maximizing the sum of agents' utilities; equivalently the utilitarian rule. In combinatorial auctions this is the winner determination problem, and it is generally computationally hard.

explainer.example: Three agents bid on combinations of items; the solver picks the set of non-overlapping bids whose total value is highest.
